To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Insecure attachment is prospectively associated with elevations in depressive symptoms.

(a) avoidant and anxious adult attachment styles predict prospective elevations in symptoms of depression but not anxiety; and (b) the association between anxious attachment and anxiety symptoms is concurrent.
Insecure adult attachment was associated with prospective elevations in emotional distress symptoms, including anxiety and depression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of adult attachment in the development of emotional distress.

the question of why insecurely attached individuals are at risk for emotional distress and, in particular, whether cognitive risk factors (i.e., dysfunctional attitudes, low self-esteem) and interpersonal stress generation processes mediate the relation between insecurely attached individuals and their risk of emotional distress.
the role of adult attachment and its implications for understanding emotional distress symptoms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cognitive risk and stress generation models provide a more comprehensive and detailed account of the relation between attachment dimensions and emotional distress than do the cognitive vulnerability and stress sensitivity models.
insecure attachment is associated with a higher risk of depressive and anxious symptoms, and that this association is mediated by a combination of cognitive and interpersonal risk factors.
attachment insecurity is a risk factor for depression and anxiety, but the specific mechanisms of how it operates depend on which specific symptoms are being examined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
insecurely attached people are at greater risk for developing emotional distress symptoms, in part, because they experience more interpersonal stressors and are more prone to cognitive vulnerability.

insecurely attached people have a greater tendency to experience interpersonal and achievement stressors, and when they experience these stressors they are more likely to experience depressive and anxious symptoms because they have a greater tendency toward dysfunctional attitudes and low levels of self-esteem.

the interpersonal stress generation mechanism explains why insecure attachment predicts both anxiety and depression, whereas the cognitive risk factors pathway explains why insecure attachment only predicts depression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mechanisms that explain why people become depressed and/or anxious are different for people who are securely versus insecurely attached.
attachment insecurity is associated with both cognitive and interpersonal mediators of emotional distress.

the cognitive risk factors model is more strongly supported for depressive symptoms than anxiety symptoms, whereas the interpersonal stress generation pathway is supported for both depression and anxiety symptoms.
